deed: Jacob Rodrigues Pereira taught deaf children to communicate in 18th-century France
title: Jacob Rodrigues Pereira, son of Marranos, taught the deaf to speak and presented his method before the King of France

trailer.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Jacob Rodrigues Pereira was the first teacher of the deaf in France.
He was a Portuguese-French Jewish educator,
the son of Marranos, who fled Portugal in 1741 to live openly as a Jew in France.
According to Jewish Currents, he had a deaf-mute sister, and to communicate with her he invented signs for numbers and punctuation.
In 1746 he taught the deaf-mute son of a wealthy French family to speak,
and in 1749 he presented his method before the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in the following year Louis the 15th granted him 800 pounds as a mark of esteem.

glance.label: Where
glance.value: Bordeaux, a Benedictine abbey in Normandy, Paris

paragraphs.text: According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Pereira was born into a Marrano family.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he was born on April 11, 1715.
He was baptized with the name Francisco Antonio Rodrigues, and he later signed several pamphlets in Spain with this name.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, after the father's death the mother fled Portugal with her son, so that she would not be accused of having relapsed into heresy.
According to Harlan Lane, in 1741 the family reached safety in Bordeaux.
There a large colony of Marranos was allowed to live openly and hold full rights, in return for 110,000 livres it paid to the crown.

stations.title: A deaf sister and a first pupil

paragraphs.text: According to Harlan Lane, in the Age of Enlightenment the deaf were thought to have no language.
They were therefore an embarrassment to the definition of man as a creature with language.
According to JTA, the Talmud placed deaf Jews together with the intellectually disabled as exempt from religious commandments.
According to Lane, Pereira's interest in the deaf first appeared when he was a youth of nineteen.
According to Jewish Currents, he had a deaf-mute sister, and to communicate with her he invented signs for numbers and punctuation.
The History-Computer website tells the same story, and presents it as a legend.
According to Lane, in Bordeaux Pereira opened a small school and began to teach speech to his first deaf pupil, his sister.
According to Lane, his second pupil was Aaron Beaumarin, a thirteen-year-old apprentice tailor who was born profoundly deaf.
In one hundred lessons over a year, Pereira taught him to articulate all the basic speech sounds and several more words.
According to Harlan Lane, at a Benedictine abbey in Normandy Pereire found an eighteen-year-old boy, the son of d'Étavigny.
The boy could read, write and sign, but not speak.
According to Jewish Currents, in 1746 Pereira taught him to speak using the method of finger-spelling, dactylology.
According to Lane, the contract the boy's father dictated to him was so strict that no teacher of the deaf since has received such a contract.
The father required Pereire to leave his family and closet himself with the boy at the abbey, alongside the prior.
According to Lane, after four months of instruction the prior convened the Royal Academy of Letters at Caen to bear witness to the pupil's progress.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, on January 19, 1747, Pereira received from the academy at Caen the first testimonial for his work, after ten years of study of anatomy and physiology and numerous experiments on the congenitally deaf.
According to Lane, after eleven months the pupil, according to a written testimonial, spoke 1,300 words that he understood, and many sentences.
According to Jewish Currents, Pereira expanded the manual alphabet of Juan Pablo Bonet and added 30 hand shapes to it.
Each shape corresponds to a sound, not to a letter.
According to Harlan Lane, he gave short, frequent lessons and used a special finger alphabet.
According to Lane, Pereira was a tireless teacher.
He strode back and forth, circled his pupils and arranged their speech organs with his hands.

According to Harlan Lane, the Academy of Sciences report on Pereire acknowledged that the art of teaching speech to the deaf did not begin with him: Wallis in England and Amman in Holland had practiced it with success about a century earlier.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, he strove to educate every pupil, regardless of social class, to the maximum level he could reach in relation to his probable future.

stations.title: Before the scholars and the king

paragraphs.text: According to Harlan Lane, about a year after he returned to Normandy at the beginning of 1748, Pereira brought his pupil to Paris.
There he presented him before the Academy of Sciences, the most prestigious scholarly body in France.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in 1749 he set forth his method before the academy in a written memoir.
According to Lane, the commission appointed by the academy included Georges Buffon, who was then writing the "Natural History of Man" and inserted into it praise of Pereira and his method.
The commission found that the art of teaching the mute to read and speak, as Pereira practiced it, was ingenious, of great public benefit and worthy of the strongest encouragement.
According to Lane, Pereira's brother described the meeting with the king in a letter: the pupil's performance lasted more than half an hour before the king left.

According to Harlan Lane, the next day Pereira and his pupil were called back, so that the ladies of the court, whom the Dauphin (the heir to the throne) had brought from Versailles too late, could also see the talking mute.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in the following year Louis the 15th granted Pereire 800 pounds as a mark of esteem.

stations.title: The pupils, the secret and the memory

paragraphs.text: According to Harlan Lane, none of Pereira's later pupils excelled like Saboureux, who became an enthusiastic spokesman for his method.
The commission found that Saboureux pronounced clearly all the sounds of French, understood common expressions and instructions in writing, and read aloud.
Marie Marois was mute and a signer when she came to him, and in her years with him she learned to speak fluently, to write letters correctly and to read easily.
In 1777 Emperor Joseph II visited Paris and asked to meet Pereira and Marie Marois, his best pupil.
According to Lane, near his death Pereira entrusted his secret method to Marie Marois, and swore her to reveal it only to his son Isaac, who was then a child.
According to History-Computer, he took his method with him to the grave when he died in 1780.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he died in Paris on September 15, 1780.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, his method was the foundation for all modern improvements, and was reintroduced in the generation of the entry's authors.
According to JTA, citing the journal The Jewish Deaf, education of the deaf improved in recent centuries in large part thanks to Jewish pioneers such as Jacob Rodrigues Pereira.
Pereira was commemorated on a Portuguese coin from 1981, marking the UN International Year of Disabled Persons.
According to Jewish Currents, Bordeaux has a street named after him.

stations.title: Scholar and intercessor for the community

paragraphs.text: According to Harlan Lane, Pereira also knew Hebrew, Portuguese, Spanish and Italian.
According to Jewish Currents, he was well-versed in finance, mathematics and physics, and designed and built an early calculating machine.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, in 1753 his proposals for increasing the speed of sailing vessels received honorable mention.
According to History-Computer, in 1772 he published a Tahitian vocabulary for the voyage of Louis-Antoine de Bougainville.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in 1765 he was appointed royal interpreter for Spanish and Portuguese.
Jewish Currents describes Pereire as an unofficial diplomat of the Jews of Portugal in France.
According to Lane, he negotiated with the government to establish a Jewish cemetery, and in 1780 he bought the land for the cemetery of the Portuguese Jews at La Villette in Paris.
According to History-Computer, on November 5, 1766, he married his kinswoman Miryam Lopes Dias, who was then 19.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, his grandson Isaac Pereire was a financier born in Bordeaux in 1806; he and his brother Emile built the railway from Paris to St.-Germain, the first line in France intended for passenger transport, which opened in 1837.
According to History-Computer, Pereira was buried in the Cimetière de la Villette, and in 1876 his remains were transferred to the Montmartre cemetery.

stations.title: What did not succeed, and what is disputed

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, his foreign birth, his Jewish faith and a certain timidity all worked against him.
According to Harlan Lane, the duke hoped that a chair would be created for Pereira at the Royal College to train disciples, but the plan was not realized.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, on November 21, 1778, the council passed a decree that placed the school for the deaf of the Abbé de l'Épée, Pereire's rival, under the protection of Louis the 16th.

According to Lane, d'Étavigny, his pupil's father, at first chose not to entrust his son to Pereire, perhaps because of the cost or for fear of entrusting his education to a Jew, and obtained a copy of Amman's treatise; only after a year without progress did he come to terms and sign a contract with Pereire.
Harlan Lane wrote his book in the voice of a deaf man, and he describes Pereira as the leading oralist who challenged the Abbé de l'Épée.
In his words, Pereira was the greatest "demutiser", celebrated by scientists and kings, and he provoked de l'Épée into publishing.
Lane relates that the speech of the pupil from the abbey in Normandy regressed when Pereire was not at his side.
In his words, this is a hallmark of oral education of those born deaf: it must be continued without a break, or the speech degenerates.
Lane argues that no person born deaf has ever permanently replaced signs with speech.
Describing oral teachers in general, he wrote ironically that the more the method is kept secret, the more people will believe in its power.
